# transfr.one

Temporary file transfer over plain HTTP. Upload a file with one request, get a
link back, share the link. Files are deleted after {{TTL_LABEL}}. No account, no
API key, no client to install.

Three ways to send:

- File: upload, then share the link. Stored for {{TTL_LABEL}}. (Upload, Download)
- Pipe: sender and receiver connected live. Nothing is stored. (Pipe)
- Stream: a stored file that keeps growing while others read it. (Stream)

## Upload

PUT or POST the file's bytes to {{ORIGIN}}/<file name>. The reply is status 200
and its body is the link, as plain text on one line.

    curl --upload-file ./report.pdf {{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf
    {{ORIGIN}}/3f1c9b27d4e0-68d0f3a2/report.pdf

Every upload gets a new link, even with a name used before. Percent-encode
spaces and special characters in the name. With curl, ending the URL in "/"
uses the local file's name and encodes it for you:

    curl --upload-file "./q3 report (final).csv" {{ORIGIN}}/

These work too:

    curl --data-binary @report.pdf {{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf
    curl -F file=@report.pdf {{ORIGIN}}/
    echo "some text" | curl --data-binary @- {{ORIGIN}}/note.txt

    # Python
    link = requests.put("{{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf", data=open("report.pdf", "rb")).text.strip()

    # JavaScript
    const link = (await (await fetch("{{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf", { method: "PUT", body: file })).text()).trim()

Send "Accept: application/json" to get JSON instead of the bare link (if you
list other types too, JSON must rank above text/plain and */*). An example
reply (the values are made up):

    curl -H "Accept: application/json" --upload-file ./report.pdf {{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf
    {"url":"{{ORIGIN}}/3f1c9b27d4e0-68d0f3a2/report.pdf","raw_url":"{{ORIGIN}}/3f1c9b27d4e0-68d0f3a2/report.pdf?raw=1","name":"report.pdf","size":48213,"content_type":"application/pdf","md5":"9e107d9d372bb6826bd81d3542a419d6","expires_at":"2026-01-01T12:00:00.000Z","expires_in_seconds":86400}

- url: for people. raw_url: for programs (see Download).
- content_type: the Content-Type header you sent. If you sent none, or a
  placeholder (application/octet-stream, or the form type curl -d sends), it is
  taken from the file extension when that is a known one. Contents are never
  inspected.
- md5: of the stored bytes, to check an upload without downloading it again.
- expires_at: to the second. The link answers 404 from that moment on.

Without JSON, the same expiry time is in the reply's X-Expires-At header.

## Download

    curl -L {{ORIGIN}}/3f1c9b27d4e0-68d0f3a2/report.pdf -o report.pdf

A GET returns the file's bytes, and supports Range requests. One exception: a
request that asks for a web page gets an HTML page with a download button
instead. That means a browser opening the link (it sends "Sec-Fetch-Dest:
document"), or a client that sends "Accept: text/html" and no Sec-Fetch-Dest
header. curl, fetch() and HTTP libraries with their default headers get the
bytes.

To get the bytes whatever the headers, add ?raw=1 to the link. That is the
"raw_url" above; use it whenever a program is the reader.

A GET or HEAD reply carries X-Expires-At (when the link stops working) and an
ETag, which is the MD5 of the file in quotes.

## Pipe

Sends straight from one command to another. Nothing is stored, so there is
nothing to delete and no link that outlives the transfer. Both sides use the
same address. Either can start first: it waits, for up to {{PIPE_WAIT_LABEL}}, until
the other connects, and then the data flows. Anyone who knows the name can be
the receiver, so make it hard to guess; a random string is fine.

    curl -T ./backup.tar {{ORIGIN}}/pipe/7f3a9c-backup          # sender
    curl {{ORIGIN}}/pipe/7f3a9c-backup -o backup.tar             # receiver

A live source works too; the receiver sees bytes as they are sent:

    tail -f app.log | curl -T - {{ORIGIN}}/pipe/7f3a9c-logs
    curl -N {{ORIGIN}}/pipe/7f3a9c-logs

- The receiver gets the bytes as an ordinary download, with a Content-Length
  when the sender's is known. No special flags are needed.
- The sender's reply comes when the transfer is over: "Sent 1234 bytes".
- One sender and one receiver at a time on a name (409 pipe_busy). The name
  can be used again once a transfer is over.
- If the other side never connects: 408 pipe_timeout. If one side drops out
  mid-way, the other gets an error (502 pipe_broken, or a download cut short).
- "Sent" means the bytes were handed to the receiver's connection. A receiver
  that disconnected while it was still waiting cannot always be told apart
  from a live one, so when it matters, have the receiver confirm what it got
  (size or checksum).
- One send carries up to {{MAX_FILE_SIZE_LABEL}}.

## Stream

A file that keeps growing. The writer adds to it for as long as it likes, and
any number of readers can fetch what is there so far, only what is new, or
follow it live. Create it first; the reply has two links:

    curl -X POST {{ORIGIN}}/stream/build.log
    read: {{ORIGIN}}/stream/1a2b3c4d5e6f/build.log
    write: {{ORIGIN}}/stream/1a2b3c4d5e6f/build.log?key=5f2c...

Give out the read link. Keep the write link: whoever has it can add data.
Create with an empty request; data goes to the write link afterwards.

Write, with the write link:

    echo "step 1 done" | curl --data-binary @- "<write link>"    # add; repeat as needed
    tail -f build.log | curl -T - "<write link>"                  # or one long upload
    ./job.sh | curl -T - "<write link>&close"                     # long upload that ends the stream with the job
    echo "finished" | curl --data-binary @- "<write link>&close"  # add and end the stream
    curl -X POST "<write link>&close"                             # end the stream, adding nothing

Data can be read as soon as it arrives, also in the middle of a long upload.

Read, with the read link:

    curl "<read link>"                        # everything so far
    curl "<read link>?from=5000"              # only the bytes from offset 5000 on
    curl "<read link>?from=5000&wait=30"      # same, but wait up to 30 s if there is nothing new
    curl -N "<read link>?follow"              # everything so far, then new bytes as they arrive
    curl -N "<read link>?from=5000&follow"    # the same, starting at offset 5000

- Every read reply has X-Stream-Length, the stream's length when the reply
  was made, and X-Stream-State, "open" or "closed". The body always ends at
  X-Stream-Length (with ?follow it goes on past it).
- To poll: read with from=<the last X-Stream-Length>&wait=30, and stop once
  the state is "closed" and nothing new came back. wait is at most 60.
- ?follow ends by itself, as a normal end of the download, when the stream is
  closed, and after {{STREAM_FOLLOW_LABEL}} at the latest; reconnect with from= to carry on.
- A "Range: bytes=5000-" header selects like from=5000; it is answered 206
  with a Content-Range, where from= is answered 200.
- A stream link always returns the bytes, to browsers too; there is no HTML
  page, ETag or md5 for a stream. The write link can also be read from.
- A stream can only be added to and closed: not changed, and not deleted
  before it expires.
- Its content type comes from its name, or from the Content-Type header sent
  when it is created.
- A stream holds up to {{STREAM_MAX_LABEL}}, and one write carries up to {{MAX_FILE_SIZE_LABEL}}. Past
  the limit a write gets 413 stream_full, after adding what still fit.
  One long upload that passes {{MAX_FILE_SIZE_LABEL}} gets 413 too_large the same way:
  what fitted is kept, so start another upload for the rest.
- A stream is deleted {{STREAM_IDLE_LABEL}} after its last write, and {{STREAM_MAX_TTL_LABEL}} after it was
  created at the latest. Closing it counts as a write. X-Expires-At on every
  reply says when.
- With "Accept: application/json", create replies {"url", "write_url", "name",
  "content_type", "length", "state", "expires_at"} and a write replies
  {"appended", "length", "state"}.
- Writes are rate limited (see Limits): about two a second from one address.
  For a faster flow of data, use one long upload.

## Encrypt (optional)

The server never needs to see the contents. Encrypt before uploading:

    gpg -c -o- report.pdf | curl --data-binary @- {{ORIGIN}}/report.pdf.pgp
    curl -L <link> | gpg -d -o report.pdf

A file whose name ends in .pgp, .gpg or .asc can also be decrypted in the
browser, on the page its link opens.

## Limits

- Size: up to {{MAX_FILE_SIZE_LABEL}} ({{MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES}} bytes). Form uploads (curl -F) and
  uploads sent without a Content-Length: up to {{MAX_BUFFERED_FILE_SIZE_LABEL}}.
- Lifetime of a file: {{TTL_LABEL}}. After that the link answers 404. A file cannot be
  deleted earlier, replaced or listed. (A stream's lifetime is in Stream; a
  pipe keeps nothing.)
- The link is the only protection. It cannot be guessed, and anyone who has it
  can download the file. Treat it like a password.
- File names: up to 256 characters, and may contain "/". Not allowed: control
  characters, and empty, "." or ".." path segments. The name becomes part of
  the link. A stream's name cannot contain "/".
- Sending: about 20 uploads, pipe sends and new streams a minute, counted
  together, from one address, and about 120 writes a minute to existing
  streams. More than that gets 429 rate_limited; wait a minute. Reading is
  not limited.

## Errors

Errors are one line of plain text that says what to change. A short code that
does not change is in the X-Error-Code header. With "Accept: application/json"
the body is JSON instead: {"error": "<the text>", "code": "<the code>", "status": 400}

- 400  no_filename, empty_body, invalid_filename, filename_too_long,
       length_mismatch (the body was not as long as its Content-Length),
       invalid_form, no_file_in_form, invalid_offset, body_not_allowed (data
       sent while creating a stream), upload_interrupted
- 403  write_key_required, wrong_write_key: writing to a stream needs its write link
- 404  not_found: the link is wrong, or the file or stream has expired
- 405  method_not_allowed: only GET, HEAD, PUT, POST and OPTIONS are supported
- 408  pipe_timeout: the other side of the pipe never connected
- 409  pipe_busy, stream_closed
- 413  too_large: the file or request is larger than the limit; stream_full
- 416  range_not_satisfiable
- 429  rate_limited
- 502  pipe_broken: the other side of the pipe disconnected

## For AI agents

- Uploading needs a tool that can send PUT or POST, such as curl in a shell. A
  tool that can only fetch pages can download a file but not upload one.
- To share a file with a person, give them the link. To hand a file to another
  program, give it the raw_url (the link with ?raw=1 added).
- This page is also served at {{ORIGIN}}/llms.txt. The source is at
  https://github.com/repalash/transfr-cf-worker
